raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
Additionally to https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8749 another precision issue

Porting this from @seanbell's https://github.com/Snowflake-AI-Research/Arctic-Platform/pull/371


**An accumulation boundary is not necessarily an optimizer step.** A caller can finish several requests with `engine.set_gradient_accumulation_boundary(True)` while delaying `engine.step()` until all requests have contributed. ZeRO-1/2 must retain every request's gradients until that update and must not carry a previous update's gradients into the next one.

This fixes both non-offloaded and CPU-offloaded optimizer paths in `deepspeed/runtime/zero/stage_1_and_2.py`, without changing configuration defaults or adding an application-side workaround.

## Root Cause And Fix

- Non-offloaded optimizers cleared `all_grad_tensors` at every boundary, discarding earlier requests before `step()`. Retain the accumulated tensors until the existing step cleanup. When the separate `param.grad_accum` tensor is cumulative, keep the existing reread behavior so reentrant checkpoint phases do not double-count gradients.
- CPU-offloaded optimizers with FP32 master weights skipped refreshing the persistent host accumulator on a step's first backward when that backward was also a boundary. A subsequent request could then add the previous step's stored gradients. Track each parameter's participation in the current update window instead of relying on the global `micro_step_id`. A first non-boundary contribution refreshes the host accumulator; a first boundary contribution uses only the existing optimizer-partition copy. If another backward follows before `step()`, recover the previous locally owned partition fragment in the accumulation dtype, then allocate or refresh the auxiliary host accumulator. Never reuse a prior update's sum.

**A single-backward update needs no auxiliary allocation or copy.** `_offload_partition_only_param_ids` records FP32-master parameters whose current sum lives only in the optimizer partition. Explicit finalization leaves those already-current gradients intact. `step()` clears both participation sets before either a successful update or an overflow return. Multiple backwards still need an auxiliary accumulator once the second contribution arrives; this change does not claim a speedup for that workload.

**Low-precision masters use a shared buffer instead of the separate FP32-master accumulator.** Their CPU accumulator is a view of the optimizer partition's gradient buffer. On a parameter's first use at a boundary, the existing boundary copy initializes that shared buffer directly, so a second host copy is unnecessary. Register the view and the parameter's participation even when skipping the extra copy; later backwards accumulate into the current window and explicit finalization can restore the shared gradient. A first non-boundary use still initializes the accumulator through the offload helper.

These changes address the [stale-gradient first-use review](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8949#discussion_r4419121849), the [low-precision boundary-handling clarification](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8949#discussion_r4419154211), and the subsequent single-backward allocation/copy concern. The code names `first_use` and `boundary` explicitly and distinguishes shared-buffer accumulation from the lazily allocated FP32-master accumulator.

**This complements DeepSpeed [#8749](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8749), rather than replacing its precision fix.** #8749 preserves FP32 partition gradients, including CPU offload. The remaining defect concerns the lifetime of accumulated gradients when model and accumulation dtypes match. [Arctic-Platform #371](https://github.com/Snowflake-AI-Research/Arctic-Platform/pull/371) motivated the native DeepSpeed repair; AP-specific hooks are not needed by this change.

## Regression Coverage

The existing `tests/unit/v1/zero/test_zero2_offload_multi_backward.py` now includes a 16-case, two-rank integration matrix:

| Axis | Cases |
| --- | --- |
| ZeRO stage | 1, 2 |
| Optimizer placement | Non-offloaded, CPU offload |
| BF16 model gradient accumulation | BF16, FP32 |
| Activation checkpointing | Disabled, reentrant |

**Each case checks independently derived gradients and actual parameter updates.** Two independent linear projections exercise partition ownership; analytical input-column sums supply the gradient reference and ordinary PyTorch SGD supplies the update reference. Binary-exact fixture values allow zero-tolerance assertions without loosening numerical thresholds.

Eight successive update windows cover a multi-call request, a zero-loss request followed by useful work, consecutive single-call requests, mixed request lengths, a boundary-first request followed by a multi-backward request, a fresh single backward after earlier updates, and two conditional-participation windows. Each projection is absent from the first backward of one window, then contributes repeatedly after having participated in the preceding update. The integration tests compare actual consecutive-single-backward updates; a separate storage regression checks the resource contract.

The existing gradient-safety suite also checks first use after another parameter's backward, with FP32 and BF16 master buffers and boundary/non-boundary first contributions. It checks the summed gradient and actual Adam update against an independent PyTorch optimizer, including a boundary-only overflow after an earlier update has allocated the auxiliary buffer. Additional controls check repeated finalization, partial partition ownership, BF16 accumulation rounding, pending pageable-source copies, and no additional storage or copy for consecutive single-boundary updates. These storage-level tests bypass the ZeRO constructor; they do not claim CPUAdam integration coverage for BF16 master weights.

## Validation

**All reported execution was on CPU, not on GPU.** Hardware: one visible Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C socket, 96 logical CPUs; two CPU/Gloo ranks for distributed cases; no GPU or accelerator driver used. Software: PyTorch `2.9.1+cu130`, DeepSpeed `0.19.8+0fe2dfcc7`, Python from `/home/yak/miniconda3/envs/dev/bin/python`. The CUDA-enabled PyTorch build does not constitute CUDA hardware validation.

| Test | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Plain request-boundary matrix before the original source fix | 4 BF16-accumulation failures, 4 FP32-accumulation passes |
| Delayed-participation offload regressions before the review fix | 2 BF16-accumulation failures, 2 FP32-accumulation passes |
| First-use storage regressions before the review fix | 4 failures (FP32/BF16 masters, boundary/non-boundary first use); 4 ordinary-accumulation controls passed |
| Single-boundary allocation/copy regression before the lazy fix | 1 FP32-master failure; 9 other storage controls passed |
| Complete request-boundary/checkpoint matrix after the lazy fix | 16 passed |
| Existing multi-backward/offload controls after the lazy fix | 10 passed |
| Gradient-safety suite after the lazy fix, including overflow | 52 passed, 2 CUDA-only skips |
| Temporary CPU storage-lifetime and allocation/copy probes | 6 passed |

The repository suites total 78 passes and 2 CUDA-only skips; the temporary probes add 6 passes. The integration matrix completed in 88.91 seconds, native optimizer controls in 105.38 seconds, the final gradient-safety rerun in 8.63 seconds, and the final temporary probes in 2.51 seconds. These are test durations, not training-throughput measurements.

New matrix command, from the DeepSpeed checkout:

```bash
DS_ACCELERATOR=cpu PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  /home/yak/miniconda3/envs/dev/bin/python -m pytest -sv \
  tests/unit/v1/zero/test_zero2_offload_multi_backward.py \
  -k multiple_request_boundaries --tb=short --color=no
```

The existing optimizer controls initially timed out with optional shared-memory communication enabled. They passed using real Gloo with only that optional communication extension disabled. The temporary test launcher contains:

```python
import sys
import deepspeed.ops
import pytest

deepspeed.ops.__compatible_ops__["deepspeed_shm
```

```bash
DS_ACCELERATOR=cpu PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  /home/yak/miniconda3/envs/dev/bin/python \
  /tmp/codex-01a13767-deepspeed-gloo-tests.py -sv \
  tests/unit/v1/zero/test_zero2_offload_multi_backward.py \
  -k TestZeroOffloadMultiBackward --tb=short --color=no

DS_ACCELERATOR=cpu PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
  /home/yak/miniconda3/envs/dev/bin/python -m pytest -sv \
  tests/unit/v1/zero/test_zero2_gradient_safety.py --tb=short --color=no
```

The configured pre-commit hooks passed for all three changed Python files and this local description, including YAPF, flake8, license, and accelerator/distributed-import checks. The first run applied YAPF's required wrapping to the new tests; the second run passed without modifications. `git diff --check` passed.

## Single-Backward Allocation And Copy Control

**The lazy fix restores the original single-boundary resource behavior in a CPU-only fixture.** For a fresh FP32-master optimizer with 1,048,576 BF16 gradient values, 12 single-boundary calls produced the following counts. The original base is `8d4f29c75`; the eager review-fix head is `7e00e1a8e`. The fixture resets per-update participation between calls and measures persistent auxiliary tensor storage and `copy_` operations, not process peak memory or GPU transfers.

| Revision | Auxiliary host bytes | Copies per boundary call |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Original base | 0 | 1 |
| Eager review fix | 2,097,152 | 2 |
| Lazy fix | 0 | 1 |

BF16-master controls remain at zero auxiliary bytes and one copy per call in all three revisions. A buffer allocated by an earlier multi-backward update remains available for reuse, but a later single-boundary update does not refresh that stale buffer. The repository regression `test_single_boundary_offload_avoids_auxiliary_storage_and_copy` checks the no-extra-storage/copy contract and actual consecutive Adam updates.

The larger allocation/copy comparison and four ordinary success/overflow storage-lifetime controls were run with the temporary probe `/tmp/codex-01a13767-pr8949-additional-feedback.py`:

```bash
DS_ACCELERATOR=cpu PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONPATH=.:tests \
  /home/yak/miniconda3/envs/dev/bin/python \
  /tmp/codex-01a13767-pr8949-additional-feedback.py
```

Synthetic CPU timings are not evidence of accelerator throughput. No end-to-end speedup is claimed.

## Compatibility And Remaining Validation

**The CPU runs validate optimizer-placement logic, not physical GPU optimizer placement or GPU-to-CPU transfers.** The regression is also enabled on hosts with at least two CUDA devices, but GPU execution remains required before claiming on-device coverage. FP16, CPUAdam integration with low-precision master weights, NVMe offload, vendor accelerators, and tensor/pipeline/expert/sequence parallelism were not validated by the new matrix. BF16 master-buffer behavior was validated only in the gradient-safety fixture described above.

Static sibling inspection found that ZeRO-3 refreshes the first microstep's partition buffer and that the BF16 optimizer retains accumulation until its update or explicit zeroing. This PR changes neither implementation. Conditional participation after the first microstep was not validated for ZeRO-3; the inspected code is not evidence that every sibling accumulation case is correct.

Full-model convergence, throughput, and peak-memory measurements were not performed. Only the fixture's auxiliary-allocation and copy-count reductions above are established. GPU transfer cost and performance for repeated-backward workloads remain unmeasured.

## Related Work And Submission

Public open-PR searches for `gradient accumulation`, `stale gradients`, and `8749 in:body`, plus the #8749 discussion, were checked on October 29, 2026. No competing request-boundary fix was identified. Related [#8728](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8728) clears unowned offload scratch for low-precision masters; [#8856](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8856) repairs the BF16 full-gradient setter. Neither supplies this per-parameter request-lifetime fix. Repeat the duplicate check before opening another PR.

AI assistance was used. A human submitter must review every changed line, run the relevant accelerator tests, and provide any required sign-off. This is the local description for existing PR #8949, excluded from the source commit; GitHub PR text is not edited by this task.

Read at `e5d68d99`.

This looks right to me. My main question going in was whether restoring only the locally owned fragment, then reducing again, would divide an already averaged previous sum by the DP size a second time. `test_multiple_request_boundaries_before_step` settles it: DP=2, expected gradients summed over requests of the per-request rank mean, exact equality, including parameters first used after another backward.

On CPU (gloo), at this head:
- All 16 `test_multiple_request_boundaries_before_step` cases pass, along with the new unit tests in `test_zero2_gradient_safety.py`.
- With the same test files on master, the 8 bf16-accumulation request-boundary cases fail; the 8 fp32-accumulation cases already pass there, since that path rereads `grad_accum`. The new unit tests (owned-fragment recovery, first use after another backward, waiting on the pageable source) fail on master as well.
- The only failures at this head are the existing `TestZeroOffloadMultiBackward` cases, which need the fused Adam op that I can't build here.

In the end-to-end test only bf16 accumulation fails on master, with or without offload. Is fp32 accumulation affected in any case? If not, saying so in the description would help users tell whether they were hit.

Follow-up to my review above. #8964 names two cases this branch doesn't cover, and I confirmed both with this PR's own request-boundary harness under CPU offload:
- a parameter used only in a non-boundary backward of a request;
- a parameter unused for a whole window and then used again.

Both give wrong gradients here with offload, as they do on master; without offload they pass. In the second, the parameter has a nonzero gradient at a step where no backward used it, which the description rules out ("must not carry a previous update's gradients into the next one"). Details are on #8964.

The larger allocation/copy comparison and four ordinary success/overflow storage-lifetime controls were run with the temporary probe `/tmp/codex-01a13767-pr8949-additional-feedback.py`:

```bash
DS_ACCELERATOR=cpu PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 PYTHONPATH=.:tests \
  /home/yak/miniconda3/envs/dev/bin/python \
  /tmp/codex-01a13767-pr8949-additional-feedback.py
```

Synthetic CPU timings are not evidence of accelerator throughput. No end-to-end speedup is claimed.

## Compatibility And Remaining Validation

**The CPU runs validate optimizer-placement logic, not physical GPU optimizer placement or GPU-to-CPU transfers.** The regression is also enabled on hosts with at least two CUDA devices, but GPU execution remains required before claiming on-device coverage. FP16, CPUAdam integration with low-precision master weights, NVMe offload, vendor accelerators, and tensor/pipeline/expert/sequence parallelism were not validated by the new matrix. BF16 master-buffer behavior was validated only in the gradient-safety fixture described above.

Static sibling inspection found that ZeRO-3 refreshes the first microstep's partition buffer and that the BF16 optimizer retains accumulation until its update or explicit zeroing. This PR changes neither implementation. Conditional participation after the first microstep was not validated for ZeRO-3; the inspected code is not evidence that every sibling accumulation case is correct.

Full-model convergence, throughput, and peak-memory measurements were not performed. Only the fixture's auxiliary-allocation and copy-count reductions above are established. GPU transfer cost and performance for repeated-backward workloads remain unmeasured.

## Related Work And Submission

Public open-PR searches for `gradient accumulation`, `stale gradients`, and `8749 in:body`, plus the #8749 discussion, were checked on October 29, 2026. No competing request-boundary fix was identified. Related [#8728](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8728) clears unowned offload scratch for low-precision masters; [#8856](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/pull/8856) repairs the BF16 full-gradient setter. Neither supplies this per-parameter request-lifetime fix. Repeat the duplicate check before opening another PR.

AI assistance was used. A human submitter must review every changed line, run the relevant accelerator tests, and provide any required sign-off. This is the local description for existing PR #8949, excluded from the source commit; GitHub PR text is not edited by this task.

+class RequestBoundaryModel(torch.nn.Module):
+
+    def __init__(self, checkpointed):
+        super().__init__()
+        self.projections = torch.nn.ModuleList([torch.nn.Linear(4, 4, bias=False), torch.nn.Linear(4, 2, bias=False)])
+        self.checkpointed = checkpointed
+
+    def forward(self, inputs, projection_indices=(0, 1)):
+        loss = inputs.new_zeros(())
+        for projection_index in projection_indices:
+            projection = self.projections[projection_index]
+            if self.checkpointed:
+                outputs = checkpoint(projection, inputs, use_reentrant=True)
+            else:
+                outputs = projection(inputs)
+            loss = loss + outputs.sum()
+        return loss

With CPU offload and FP32 master weights, if a parameter was used in the previous optimizer step but is first used only after another backward in the current step (for example, a conditionally selected expert), `micro_step_id > 0` causes `async_accumulate_grad_in_cpu_via_gpu()` to add the persistent `accumulated_grads_in_cpu[param_id]` from the previous step. Determine whether the parameter is already active in the current window via `_offload_accumulated_param_ids`, and overwrite rather than accumulate on its first use.

This looks right to me. My main question going in was whether restoring only the locally owned fragment, then reducing again, would divide an already averaged previous sum by the DP size a second time. `test_multiple_request_boundaries_before_step` settles it: DP=2, expected gradients summed over requests of the per-request rank mean, exact equality, including parameters first used after another backward.

On CPU (gloo), at this head:
- All 16 `test_multiple_request_boundaries_before_step` cases pass, along with the new unit tests in `test_zero2_gradient_safety.py`.
- With the same test files on master, the 8 bf16-accumulation request-boundary cases fail; the 8 fp32-accumulation cases already pass there, since that path rereads `grad_accum`. The new unit tests (owned-fragment recovery, first use after another backward, waiting on the pageable source) fail on master as well.
- The only failures at this head are the existing `TestZeroOffloadMultiBackward` cases, which need the fused Adam op that I can't build here.

In the end-to-end test only bf16 accumulation fails on master, with or without offload. Is fp32 accumulation affected in any case? If not, saying so in the description would help users tell whether they were hit.

Follow-up to my review above. #8964 names two cases this branch doesn't cover, and I confirmed both with this PR's own request-boundary harness under CPU offload:
- a parameter used only in a non-boundary backward of a request;
- a parameter unused for a whole window and then used again.

Both give wrong gradients here with offload, as they do on master; without offload they pass. In the second, the parameter has a nonzero gradient at a step where no backward used it, which the description rules out ("must not carry a previous update's gradients into the next one"). Details are on #8964.
